tables.caption: Table 1: Comparison of related methods with its forecasting capability. The character “.” in the Transformers denotes the name of *former. The character ✧ indicates that the model can be applied to multivariate forecasting scenarios but not explicitly model the cross-variate dependency.

Table 2: Full results of the short-term forecasting task on EPF dataset. We follow the standard protocol in short-term electricity price forecasting, where the input length and predict length are set to 168 and 24 respectively for all baselines. Avg means the average results from all five datasets.

Table 3: Multivariate forecasting results. We compare extensive competitive models under different prediction lengths following the setting of iTransformer [ 23 ] . The look-back length L L is set to 96 for all baselines. Results are averaged from all prediction lengths S = { 96,192,336,720 } S=\{96,192,336,720\} .
Table 4: Ablation Results. Ex. and En. are abbreviations for Exogenous variable and Endogenous variable. P , G and V denote patch token, learnable global token, and variate token respectively.
Table 5: Model performance under missing values. Zeros and Random represent the cases that the corresponding series is set as zeros or random values respectively.
Table 6: Dataset descriptions. Ex . and En. are abbreviations for the Exogenous variable and Endogenous variable, respectively. The dataset size is organized in (Train, Validation, Test)
Table 7: Model performance with overlapped patches.
Table 8: Ablation study on long-term forecast.
Table 9: More baselines in the short-term forecasting with exogenous variables task.
Table 10: More baselines in the multivariate long-term forecasting. ‘-’ denotes there is no officially reported results.
Table 11: Full results of the long-term forecasting with exogenous variables task. “-” denotes out of memory (OOM) problem.
Table 12: Full results of the long-term multivariate forecasting task.
